page: Amazon Web Services c7i-flex.xlarge is a burstable compute-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor and x86_64 architecture. It features an Intel Xeon 8488C processor running at 3.2 GHz with 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores and 2 threads per core. The processor includes 105 MB of L3 cache along with support for advanced instruction sets including AVX-512 and Intel AMX (Advanced Matrix Extensions) for int8 and bfloat16 vector operations. System memory consists of 8.0 GB of DDR5 RAM operating at 5 GHz, providing a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU core. The server has no local NVMe storage and provides a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps with zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark results reflect the burstable CPU allocation profile and resource constraints of the instance. Single-threaded performance reaches average levels, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2032.08 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1912.0. In contrast, multi-threaded CPU workloads score in the bottom 25% bracket, as evidenced by a stress-ng multi-core result of 4216.75 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 4231.0. Memory sub-system performance is constrained, yielding a PassMark memory score of 978.31 (bottom 10%) and uncached memory read bandwidth of 25.92 GB/sec. Despite memory bandwidth limitations, static web serving throughput hits an average 7.82 GB/sec, while LLM text generation for small 135M parameter models achieves an average rate of 112.75 tokens per second.

The c7i-flex.xlarge provides qualitative cost efficiency for workloads that experience periodic usage bursts rather than sustained multi-core saturation. Given its lower RAM-to-vCPU ratio, lack of dedicated local storage, and lower multi-threaded score, it is less suited for heavy database operations (PassMark database score of 2362.48) or parallel software compilation (Geekbench clang score of 4755.0). Instead, the instance fits light web serving, general-purpose microservices, single-threaded processing tasks, and development environments requiring modern Intel AVX-512 or AMX instruction extensions without demanding continuous full-core CPU performance.
